objective_text: Diagnose physical interface and cabling faults.
question_instruction: Select the BEST corrective action for the evidence shown.
question_text: Users connected through this switch port report very slow transfers even though the link remains up. Which corrective action best addresses the evidence?
answer_a: Increase the interface maximum transmission unit on both endpoints.
answer_b: Configure both endpoints to use compatible speed and duplex settings, preferably through matching autonegotiation.
answer_c: Change the workstation default gateway to the switch management address.
answer_d: Enable PortFast on the switch port and clear the interface counters.
correct_explanation: Late collisions on a half-duplex link while the peer is operating full duplex are strong evidence of a duplex mismatch. Matching autonegotiation or explicitly matching speed and duplex on both endpoints resolves the Layer 1 and Layer 2 mismatch.
answer_a_explanation: An MTU change does not correct a duplex mismatch or late collisions.
answer_b_explanation: Correct. Both endpoints must agree on speed and duplex. Matching autonegotiation is normally preferred when both devices support it.
answer_c_explanation: A default-gateway change affects routed reachability, not Ethernet collision behavior on an active local link.
answer_d_explanation: PortFast changes spanning-tree transition behavior. Clearing counters removes history but does not correct the mismatch.
reference_notes: Cisco interface documentation defines speed and duplex settings and provides interface counters used to identify collision and mismatch symptoms.
author_notes: Accelerated staging approval authorized by the repository owner on 2026-08-01.

objective_text: Explain the roles of hypervisors, virtual machines, and containers.
question_text: Which statement best distinguishes an application container from a traditional virtual machine?
answer_a: A container emulates physical network cabling, while a virtual machine emulates only storage.
answer_b: A container requires a separate guest operating system for each application, while a virtual machine does not.
answer_c: A container can run only on bare-metal hardware, while a virtual machine requires a hosted operating system.
answer_d: A container packages an application while sharing the host operating-system kernel, whereas a virtual machine normally runs a guest operating system on virtual hardware.
correct_explanation: Containers use operating-system virtualization and application packaging, so multiple containers commonly share the host kernel. A virtual machine presents virtual hardware on which a separate guest operating system runs.
answer_a_explanation: Neither technology is defined by emulating physical cabling. Both can use virtual networking.
answer_b_explanation: This reverses the normal distinction. Virtual machines normally include guest operating systems, while containers share the host kernel.
answer_c_explanation: Containers and virtual machines can both run in several deployment models. Containers are not limited to bare metal.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. This captures the kernel-sharing model of containers and the guest-operating-system model of virtual machines.
reference_notes: NIST SP 800-125 describes guest operating systems running on virtual hardware. NIST SP 800-190 describes containers as operating-system virtualization combined with application packaging.
author_notes: Accelerated staging approval authorized by the repository owner on 2026-08-01.

objective_text: Troubleshoot IPv4 configuration, assignment, and subnetting.
question_text: A LAN is assigned the subnet 10.20.30.96/27. Which range contains all addresses that can be assigned to ordinary hosts in this subnet?
correct_explanation: A /27 contains 32 addresses. The block beginning at 10.20.30.96 ends at 10.20.30.127. The first address is the network address and the last is the directed broadcast address, leaving .97 through .126 for hosts.
answer_a_explanation: This range includes the network address and directed broadcast address.
answer_b_explanation: This range incorrectly removes two usable host addresses.
answer_c_explanation: This range includes 10.20.30.127, the directed broadcast address.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. The usable host range is 10.20.30.97 through 10.20.30.126.
study_topics: IPv4 subnetting|CIDR|Network address|Broadcast address|Usable host range
reference_notes: CIDR prefix /27 leaves five host bits, producing 32-address blocks. Programmatic check: network 10.20.30.96, broadcast 10.20.30.127, usable .97 through .126.

objective_text: Troubleshoot IPv6 configuration, assignment, and prefix sizing.
question_text: An interface uses modified EUI-64 to build an IPv6 interface identifier from MAC address 00-25-96-12-34-56. Which interface identifier is produced?
correct_explanation: Modified EUI-64 inserts FFFE between the first and last three bytes of the MAC address and flips the universal/local bit in the first byte. The first byte changes from 00 to 02, producing 0225:96FF:FE12:3456.
answer_a_explanation: Correct. FFFE is inserted and the universal/local bit changes 00 to 02.
answer_b_explanation: This inserts FFFE but does not flip the universal/local bit.
answer_c_explanation: The inserted bytes are in the wrong order.
answer_d_explanation: This does not preserve the required EUI-64 byte grouping and bit change.
reference_notes: Cisco IPv6 addressing documentation describes modified EUI-64 construction, including insertion of FFFE and inversion of the universal/local bit.

objective_text: Select appropriate wireless bands and channels.
question_text: A small office has many nearby 2.4 GHz networks. All company laptops support both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. The administrator wants more nonoverlapping channel choices and less congestion. Which band is the better starting choice?
answer_a: 2.4 GHz, because it provides more nonoverlapping 20 MHz channels in the United States.
answer_b: 5 GHz, because it provides substantially more nonoverlapping channels for high-density planning.
answer_c: 2.4 GHz, because higher frequencies penetrate obstacles more effectively.
answer_d: 5 GHz, because every 5 GHz channel is exempt from radar-detection requirements.
correct_explanation: The 5 GHz band provides many more nonoverlapping channel choices than 2.4 GHz and is commonly preferred for higher-density deployments when clients support it.
answer_a_explanation: The 2.4 GHz band has only three commonly used nonoverlapping 20 MHz channels in the United States.
answer_b_explanation: Correct. More usable spectrum and more nonoverlapping channels make 5 GHz a strong starting point for this requirement.
answer_c_explanation: Lower frequencies generally propagate farther and penetrate obstacles better than higher frequencies.
answer_d_explanation: Some 5 GHz channels require Dynamic Frequency Selection to avoid radar systems.
reference_notes: Cisco RF guidance identifies three nonoverlapping 2.4 GHz channels and substantially more nonoverlapping 5 GHz channel options, with DFS requirements on some 5 GHz channels.

objective_text: Distinguish wireless security protocols.
question_text: Which TWO characteristics are associated with WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise rather than a personal pre-shared-key deployment?
answer_a: Client authentication can use IEEE 802.1X and Extensible Authentication Protocol.
answer_b: Every user must share the same wireless passphrase.
answer_c: The access point disables encryption after authentication succeeds.
answer_d: Authentication decisions can be processed by a centralized RADIUS server.
correct_explanation: Enterprise wireless security commonly uses 802.1X with EAP for client authentication and a centralized AAA service such as RADIUS. Personal deployments instead rely on a shared credential.
answer_a_explanation: Correct. 802.1X and EAP provide the framework for enterprise client authentication.
answer_b_explanation: A shared passphrase characterizes personal authentication rather than enterprise authentication.
answer_c_explanation: Enterprise authentication does not disable wireless encryption after login.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. RADIUS commonly centralizes authentication and related AAA decisions for enterprise wireless access.
reference_notes: Cisco wireless guidance covers WPA3 deployment context. Cisco RADIUS guidance documents centralized AAA operation used with enterprise authentication.

objective_text: Troubleshoot wired and wireless client connectivity.
question_text: A Windows laptop is configured for DHCP and receives 169.254.24.18/16. Other users on the expected corporate VLAN receive addresses in 10.40.20.0/24. What does the laptop address most strongly indicate?
answer_a: The laptop successfully received a routable address from the corporate DHCP scope.
answer_b: The laptop is using the configured default gateway as its own address.
answer_c: The laptop learned an address from IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration.
answer_d: The laptop assigned itself an Automatic Private IP Addressing address after failing to obtain a DHCP lease.
correct_explanation: Windows uses Automatic Private IP Addressing in 169.254.0.0/16 when a DHCP-configured interface cannot obtain a lease. The next investigation should focus on local link, VLAN, DHCP relay, and DHCP-server reachability.
answer_a_explanation: The expected corporate DHCP scope is 10.40.20.0/24, not the link-local 169.254.0.0/16 range.
answer_b_explanation: A host does not normally assign the default-gateway address to its own interface.
answer_c_explanation: The displayed address is IPv4 and is not produced by IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. A 169.254.x.x address on a DHCP-configured Windows client indicates APIPA fallback.
reference_notes: Microsoft documents APIPA use of 169.254.0.0/16 when DHCP is unavailable. Cisco DHCP documentation covers IOS server behavior and lease assignment.

objective_text: Troubleshoot DHCPv4 clients, servers, and relays on IOS devices.
question_text: Clients on 10.20.30.0/24 cannot obtain addresses from the DHCP server at 10.40.50.25. Routing between the two subnets works. Which configuration change is required?
answer_a: Move the ip helper-address command to GigabitEthernet0/0, the interface that receives the client broadcasts.
answer_b: Change the helper address to the GigabitEthernet0/1 interface address.
answer_c: Configure ip dhcp excluded-address on GigabitEthernet0/1.
answer_d: Remove the IP address from GigabitEthernet0/0 so broadcasts can cross the router.
correct_explanation: The DHCP relay command belongs on the Layer 3 interface that receives broadcasts from the clients. GigabitEthernet0/0 faces 10.20.30.0/24, so it must relay those broadcasts to 10.40.50.25.
answer_a_explanation: Correct. The helper is configured on the client-facing interface where DHCP broadcasts arrive.
answer_b_explanation: The helper target must be the DHCP server address, not the router interface address.
answer_c_explanation: Excluded-address configuration is used by an IOS DHCP server and does not place the relay on the correct interface.
answer_d_explanation: Removing the gateway address would break routed connectivity and would not forward broadcasts.
study_topics: DHCP relay|ip helper-address|Client broadcasts|IOS interface configuration
reference_notes: Cisco DHCP relay documentation specifies configuring the helper address on the interface that receives client broadcast requests.
author_notes: Accelerated staging approval authorized by the repository owner on 2026-08-01.

objective_text: Configure Layer 2 IEEE 802.1Q trunk interfaces.
question_text: The link is trunking and VLAN 20 traffic passes, but the switches report a native VLAN mismatch. Which change corrects the inconsistency?
answer_a: Configure both trunk ports as access ports in VLAN 20.
answer_b: Remove VLAN 99 from the allowed VLAN list on SW1.
answer_c: Configure the same native VLAN on both ends of the trunk.
answer_d: Disable Dynamic Trunking Protocol on only SW2.
correct_explanation: Both ends of an 802.1Q trunk should use the same native VLAN so untagged frames are classified consistently. SW1 uses VLAN 99 while SW2 uses VLAN 1.
answer_a_explanation: Changing both ports to access mode would remove the trunk and prevent multiple VLANs from crossing the link.
answer_b_explanation: Removing VLAN 99 from the allowed list does not make the native VLAN settings agree.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. Matching the native VLAN on both endpoints resolves the mismatch.
answer_d_explanation: Disabling trunk negotiation on one side does not change the native VLAN value.
reference_notes: Cisco trunk documentation covers native VLAN configuration, allowed VLANs, and operational verification.

objective_text: Configure Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP port channels.
question_instruction: Select the BEST configuration correction for forming an LACP port channel.
question_text: The two physical links remain stand-alone and Port-channel1 is down. Which change best corrects the negotiation mismatch?
answer_a: Change SW1 to channel-group 1 mode desirable.
answer_b: Configure both switches with channel-group 1 mode on.
answer_c: Change SW2 to channel-group 1 mode passive or active so it participates in LACP.
answer_d: Remove the channel-group commands and configure the links as routed interfaces.
correct_explanation: SW1 is configured for LACP active mode, but SW2 uses static mode on. LACP requires compatible active or passive negotiation modes on the peer. Changing SW2 to active or passive allows the bundle to form if the remaining interface parameters match.
answer_a_explanation: Desirable is associated with PAgP, not LACP.
answer_b_explanation: Static mode on can form a non-negotiated EtherChannel, but replacing LACP on both sides is not the best correction when LACP is required.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. LACP active can form with an active or passive peer.
answer_d_explanation: Removing aggregation does not meet the requirement to form an LACP port channel.
reference_notes: Cisco EtherChannel documentation defines LACP active and passive modes and distinguishes them from static mode on.

objective_text: Configure switch virtual interfaces.
question_text: A switch has interface Vlan30 configured with an IP address and no shutdown, but the line protocol remains down. The show vlan brief output does not list VLAN 30. Which action is required first?
answer_a: Configure the SVI as a routed physical port.
answer_b: Assign the SVI to the native VLAN of every trunk.
answer_c: Create VLAN 30 in the VLAN database and ensure the VLAN has an active associated port or trunk path.
answer_d: Configure an IP helper address on the SVI.
correct_explanation: An SVI depends on its VLAN existing and being operational on the switch. Creating VLAN 30 and ensuring an active Layer 2 path for that VLAN allows the SVI line protocol to come up when other conditions are satisfied.
answer_a_explanation: An SVI is a logical VLAN interface and is not converted into a physical routed port.
answer_b_explanation: The SVI VLAN does not need to be the native VLAN on every trunk.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. The VLAN must exist and have an active Layer 2 presence for the SVI protocol state to become operational.
answer_d_explanation: A helper address relays selected broadcasts and does not create the VLAN or activate the SVI.
reference_notes: Cisco VLAN and interface documentation describes VLAN creation, interface state, and switch virtual interface operation.
author_notes: Accelerated staging approval authorized by the repository owner on 2026-08-01.

objective_text: Configure edge ports for Voice over IP phones.
question_text: A Cisco IP phone connects to a switch access port, and a workstation connects through the phone. The workstation should use VLAN 20 and the phone should use voice VLAN 30. Which TWO interface commands provide the VLAN assignments?
answer_a: switchport access vlan 20
answer_b: switchport trunk native vlan 20
answer_c: switchport voice vlan 30
answer_d: switchport trunk allowed vlan 20,30
correct_explanation: A phone-plus-workstation access port uses the access VLAN for ordinary data frames from the workstation and the voice VLAN command to advertise and carry the phone voice VLAN.
answer_a_explanation: Correct. This assigns untagged workstation traffic to data VLAN 20.
answer_b_explanation: The port is not being configured as an 802.1Q trunk with a native VLAN.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. This assigns and advertises voice VLAN 30 for the IP phone.
answer_d_explanation: A normal phone edge port does not require a trunk allowed-VLAN list.

objective_text: Validate network documentation with CDP and LLDP.
question_text: A network diagram states that SW1 GigabitEthernet1/0/24 connects to router R1. CDP on that port instead reports device SW2 using remote port GigabitEthernet1/0/48. What is the best conclusion?
answer_a: CDP proves that R1 has been renamed SW2 and no documentation change is needed.
answer_b: The discovered neighbor conflicts with the diagram, so the cabling or documentation should be verified and corrected.
answer_c: The port must be an access port because CDP cannot operate across trunks.
answer_d: The switch should disable CDP so the diagram remains authoritative.
correct_explanation: CDP provides directly observed neighbor identity and interface information. A mismatch with the diagram indicates that either the physical connection or the documentation is inaccurate and needs verification.
answer_a_explanation: A different device identity and remote port should not be assumed to be a harmless rename.
answer_b_explanation: Correct. Discovery evidence should be reconciled with the intended and documented topology.
answer_c_explanation: CDP can operate on access and trunk links.
answer_d_explanation: Disabling discovery hides evidence and does not resolve the discrepancy.
reference_notes: Cisco CDP and LLDP documentation describes neighbor identity, local and remote interfaces, capabilities, and use for topology verification.

answer_d: Port-channel10

answer_b: Loop guard
answer_c: Storm control
answer_d: BPDU guard

objective_text: Interpret routing tables to determine a packet next hop.
question_text: A packet is destined for 10.20.30.200. Which next hop will the router select?
answer_a: 192.0.2.254 through GigabitEthernet0/3
answer_b: 192.0.2.1 through GigabitEthernet0/0
answer_c: 192.0.2.3 through GigabitEthernet0/2
answer_d: 192.0.2.2 through GigabitEthernet0/1
correct_explanation: The destination 10.20.30.200 falls within 10.20.30.128/25. That route is more specific than the /24, /16, and default routes, so longest-prefix matching selects next hop 192.0.2.3.
answer_a_explanation: The default route is used only when no more specific route matches.
answer_b_explanation: The /16 route matches but is less specific than the /25 route.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. 10.20.30.200 is in 10.20.30.128/25, the longest matching prefix.
answer_d_explanation: The /24 route matches but is less specific than the /25 route.

objective_text: Troubleshoot floating static routes.
question_instruction: Select the BEST route for backup use while OSPF remains preferred during normal operation.
question_text: A router learns 10.60.0.0/16 through OSPF. A backup WAN next hop at 192.0.2.6 should be used only after the OSPF route disappears. Which static route best meets the requirement?
correct_explanation: OSPF has an administrative distance of 110. A floating static route must use a higher administrative distance so it remains inactive while the OSPF route exists and becomes eligible when the OSPF route is removed.
answer_a_explanation: Administrative distance 1 would make the static route preferred over OSPF during normal operation.
answer_b_explanation: This configures a host route mask and does not represent the required /16 network.

objective_text: Configure and troubleshoot OSPF neighbor adjacencies.
question_instruction: Select the BEST corrective action for the OSPF evidence.
question_text: R1 and R2 can ping each other on the directly connected subnet, but the OSPF neighbor remains in EXSTART. Which change best addresses the evidence?
answer_a: Configure the same OSPF router ID on both routers.
answer_b: Match the interface maximum transmission unit values on the two OSPF peers.
answer_c: Change both interfaces to passive in the OSPF process.
answer_d: Configure different area IDs on the two interfaces.
correct_explanation: The peers show different interface MTU values. An OSPF MTU mismatch can prevent database-description exchange from completing and leave a neighbor in EXSTART or EXCHANGE. Matching the MTU values addresses the shown fault.
answer_a_explanation: OSPF neighbors require unique router IDs. Duplicating the router ID would create another problem.
answer_b_explanation: Correct. The displayed MTU mismatch is consistent with the EXSTART adjacency failure.
answer_c_explanation: A passive interface suppresses OSPF hello packets and would prevent adjacency formation.
answer_d_explanation: OSPF neighbors on a link must use the same area ID.
reference_notes: Cisco OSPF troubleshooting guidance identifies interface MTU mismatch as a cause of neighbors becoming stuck during database exchange.

objective_text: Configure and verify the OSPF router ID.
question_text: An OSPF router has no manually configured router ID. At process startup it has loopback addresses 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.50, plus physical-interface address 10.1.1.1. Which router ID is selected?
correct_explanation: When no manual router ID is set, OSPF prefers the highest IPv4 address on an operational loopback interface. Of the available loopbacks, 192.0.2.50 is highest.
answer_a_explanation: A physical-interface address is considered only when no eligible loopback address is available.
answer_b_explanation: This is a loopback address, but it is lower than 192.0.2.50.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. It is the highest loopback IPv4 address available at OSPF process startup.
answer_d_explanation: The router can derive a nonzero router ID from the listed interfaces.

objective_text: Diagnose name-resolution faults involving common DNS records.
question_text: A DNS administrator must support an IPv4 forward lookup for app.example.com and a reverse lookup from the server IPv4 address back to its hostname. Which TWO record types are required?

answer_d_explanation: Correct. A /32 mask identifies exactly one IPv4 destination.

objective_text: Configure OSPF on point-to-point links.
question_text: Two routers share an Ethernet link with no other OSPF routers. Which TWO statements describe configuring the OSPF network type as point-to-point on both ends?
answer_a: The routers must elect a designated router and backup designated router before exchanging routes.
answer_b: The link does not use a designated-router or backup-designated-router election.
answer_c: The two routers can form an adjacency directly when their other OSPF parameters are compatible.
answer_d: The configuration automatically places the interfaces into different OSPF areas.
correct_explanation: The OSPF point-to-point network type is designed for a two-router link. It does not elect a DR or BDR, and the peers can form a full adjacency when area, timers, authentication, addressing, and other required parameters are compatible.
answer_a_explanation: DR and BDR election is associated with OSPF broadcast and nonbroadcast multiaccess behavior, not point-to-point operation.
answer_b_explanation: Correct. Point-to-point links do not elect a DR or BDR.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. The two peers establish adjacency directly when the remaining settings agree.
answer_d_explanation: Network type does not assign interfaces to different areas.

objective_text: Configure OSPF on broadcast networks.
question_text: R2 has the highest OSPF interface priority but remains the backup designated router after its priority is increased. Why does R1 remain the designated router?
answer_a: The router with the lowest priority must remain designated router until the interface fails.
answer_b: Router IDs are ignored on Ethernet broadcast networks.
answer_c: An established OSPF DR election is nonpreemptive, so a later priority increase does not replace the current DR.
answer_d: A router with priority 100 is ineligible to become the designated router.
correct_explanation: OSPF DR and BDR elections are nonpreemptive. Raising R2’s priority after the election does not displace the existing DR. A new election requires the relevant adjacency or interface conditions to reset.
answer_a_explanation: Higher priority is preferred during an election, not lower priority.
answer_b_explanation: Router ID is used as a tiebreaker when priorities are equal.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. The current DR is not preempted by a later-arriving or newly reprioritized router.
answer_d_explanation: A positive priority such as 100 is eligible and is higher than the default priority of 1.
reference_notes: Cisco OSPF guidance explains broadcast-network election and the nonpreemptive behavior of an established DR and BDR.

objective_text: Explain IPsec remote-access and site-to-site VPNs.
question_text: Which scenario is an IPsec site-to-site VPN?
answer_a: One employee uses a VPN client to connect a laptop to the corporate network from a hotel.
answer_b: A wireless client uses WPA3-Enterprise to authenticate to an access point.
answer_c: An administrator opens an SSH session to one router.
answer_d: Two security gateways maintain an encrypted tunnel between the subnets at separate offices.
correct_explanation: A site-to-site VPN connects networks through VPN gateways, allowing hosts at each location to communicate across the protected tunnel. A user VPN client is a remote-access model.
answer_a_explanation: This is a remote-access VPN because an individual endpoint initiates the connection.
answer_b_explanation: WPA3-Enterprise protects wireless access and is not an IPsec site-to-site tunnel.
answer_c_explanation: SSH secures one management session rather than connecting two sites.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. The gateways protect traffic between the office networks.

question_text: What NAT behavior is demonstrated by the translation table?

answer_b: PAT allows multiple inside hosts to share one inside-global address by tracking different transport-layer ports.
answer_c: The router is translating only destination addresses for inbound traffic.
answer_d: The router is using an IPsec tunnel instead of address translation.

answer_c_explanation: The table shows inside source addresses and ports being translated for outbound sessions.

objective_text: Configure Dynamic ARP Inspection.
question_text: Dynamic ARP Inspection is being enabled in VLAN 20. Most clients use DHCP, but one authorized printer uses a static IPv4 address. Which TWO actions support correct validation?
answer_a: Enable DHCP snooping for VLAN 20 so dynamic client bindings can be learned.
answer_b: Mark every user-facing access port as trusted for ARP inspection.
answer_c: Provide an ARP ACL or other supported static binding information for the printer.
answer_d: Disable DHCP snooping because DAI cannot use its binding database.
correct_explanation: DAI commonly validates DHCP clients against the DHCP snooping binding database. A statically addressed device is not learned through DHCP, so an ARP ACL or supported static binding method is needed for that legitimate mapping.
answer_a_explanation: Correct. DHCP snooping supplies IP-to-MAC-to-port bindings for dynamically addressed clients.
answer_b_explanation: Trusting all access ports would allow unvalidated ARP messages from endpoints and undermine the control.
answer_c_explanation: Correct. The static printer requires explicit validation data because it does not create a DHCP snooping binding.
answer_d_explanation: DAI is designed to use the DHCP snooping binding database for dynamic hosts.

objective_text: Configure storm control.
question_text: Broadcast traffic on GigabitEthernet1/0/12 reaches 8 percent of interface bandwidth. Based on the configuration and output, what happens?
answer_a: The switch permits the traffic because the lower threshold is 3 percent.
answer_b: The switch converts the broadcasts into unicasts until usage falls below 5 percent.
answer_c: The switch places only the source MAC address into a blocked state.
answer_d: The configured shutdown action disables the port after the rising threshold is exceeded.
correct_explanation: The rising threshold is 5 percent and current broadcast traffic is 8 percent. With storm-control action shutdown configured, the threshold violation disables the interface rather than merely filtering traffic.
answer_a_explanation: The lower threshold controls recovery behavior; the rising threshold determines when the storm condition begins.
answer_b_explanation: Storm control does not convert broadcast frames into unicast frames.
answer_c_explanation: The control operates on traffic levels at the interface rather than blocking only one learned source MAC.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. Current traffic exceeds the 5 percent rising threshold and the configured action is shutdown.

answer_b: On user-facing access ports where hosts should not send router advertisements

question_text: An AI agent can investigate incidents and propose configuration changes through an automation platform. Which operating model best reduces the risk of an incorrect network change?
answer_a: Allow the agent unrestricted production access because it can process telemetry faster than people.
answer_b: Hide the proposed commands so operators are not biased by the agent output.
answer_c: Let the agent modify devices whenever its confidence score is above 50 percent.
answer_d: Limit its scope, require a reviewable change diff and human approval, and maintain validation and rollback steps.

answer_b_explanation: Operators need transparent, reviewable evidence and proposed actions.
answer_c_explanation: A confidence threshold alone is not a safe authorization model for production changes.
answer_d_explanation: Correct. Scope, oversight, validation, and rollback provide practical guardrails.
